lessons.title: Structural Breaks: When Normal Itself Changes

children.text: "Structural break" has been this course's most repeated warning, under different names in different chapters: a genuine deterioration in Chapter 1, a re-rating in Chapter 5, a falling-mean trap in Chapter 3. Every time, the same underlying event was happening. The statistical parameters describing a series, its mean, its volatility, its half-life, changed permanently, and any tool still using the old parameters started giving confidently wrong answers. This lesson stops treating structural breaks as a vague danger to watch out for and gives you concrete, practical ways to actually notice one happening.

body.text: A structural break is a permanent shift in the parameters, mean, volatility, or reversion speed, that describe a series. A tool built on Chapter 2's statistics assumes those parameters are stable. When they aren't, the tool doesn't fail loudly, it keeps producing calm, confident numbers built on assumptions that quietly stopped being true.

children.text: Watching Phi Itself, Not Just the Price

Chapter 2 estimated phi once, from a fixed window of data, and treated it as a fact about the stock. A more honest approach re-estimates phi on a rolling basis, say every 20 trading days using the trailing 60 days, and watches whether that number itself stays stable over time. A stock's phi sitting steadily around 0.85 for months describes a consistent, roughly 4.3-day half-life, a reliable reverter. Phi suddenly jumping to 0.98 or higher after some specific event is not a small change. It describes a half-life exploding from roughly 4.3 days to roughly 34 days, an eightfold increase, edging toward Lesson 3's random walk with no reliable home to return to at all.

body.title: Rolling phi estimate before and after an event (illustrative)

body.text: Phi crossing above 1 is a mathematically dramatic result. It means the deviation series is no longer even theoretically mean-reverting under the AR(1) model from Chapter 1, it is now expanding rather than decaying. A price series can still look superficially normal on a chart for weeks after this shift, while every statistic estimated from before the break is already describing a process that no longer exists.

body.code:
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

def rolling_phi(close, ma_window=20, phi_window=60, step=20, alert_threshold=0.97):
    ma = close.rolling(ma_window).mean()
    deviation = (close - ma).dropna()

    alerts = []
    for end in range(phi_window, len(deviation), step):
        window = deviation.iloc[end - phi_window:end]
        x = window.shift(1).dropna()
        y = window.loc[x.index]
        if len(x) < 10:
            continue
        phi = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)[0]
        alerts.append({"period_end": deviation.index[end - 1], "phi": round(phi, 3),
                        "possible_structural_break": phi >= alert_threshold})

    return pd.DataFrame(alerts)

print(rolling_phi(close).tail())
body.caption: Re-estimating phi on a rolling basis and flagging a possible structural break whenever it crosses a chosen threshold, here 0.97.
Five practical warning signs of a possible structural break

cells: Rolling phi jumping toward or past 1
Reversion speed itself changing, not just the price
Volatility that doesn't revert on schedule
Realized volatility staying elevated well beyond its usual half-life
The reversion target itself sliding, not staying flat
Promoter pledge activity, credit downgrades, client loss, regulatory action
A run of failed reversions on the same name
The system's own win rate on one stock degrading sharply and persistently

children.text: That last warning sign deserves its own emphasis, because it is the one signal that requires no forecasting at all. If a specific stock has generated three or four systematic signals in a row that all hit the stop-loss or timed out instead of hitting the target, that is not bad luck to shrug off. It is your own strategy directly reporting that its assumptions about this particular stock no longer hold, empirically, without needing to diagnose the specific cause.

body.title: Size the half-life explosion
body.prompt: A stock's rolling phi estimate jumps from 0.85 to 0.98 after a news event. By approximately how many trading days does its estimated half-life increase (new half-life minus old half-life, rounded to the nearest whole day)?
body.explanation: At phi = 0.85, half-life is about 4.3 days. At phi = 0.98, half-life is about 34.3 days. The increase is roughly 30 days, an eightfold jump in how long a reversion is expected to take, a dramatic signal that the old, fast-reverting regime no longer describes this stock.

body.title: Which warning sign needs no forecasting at all?
body.question: Which of this lesson's five warning signs can be detected purely from a strategy's own historical results, without needing any news, fundamental research, or forecast of what happens next?
options: A run of failed reversions on the same name
Rolling phi jumping toward or past 1
body.explanation: A run of failed reversions is visible directly from the strategy's own trade log, stops and timeouts piling up on one name, without requiring any outside research or judgment call. The other three signals are useful but require either statistical re-estimation or fundamental research to notice.

cards.definition: A permanent shift in the parameters, mean, volatility, or reversion speed, describing a series, after which statistics estimated from before the shift no longer apply.
Recomputing a statistic like phi repeatedly on a moving window of recent data, rather than once on a fixed historical sample, to detect when the underlying process itself has changed.
A run of consecutive stop-loss or timeout exits on the same stock, treated as direct, empirical evidence that a strategy's assumptions about that stock no longer hold.

points: A structural break is a permanent change in the parameters describing a series, not just a large price move, and it makes every statistic estimated from before the break unreliable going forward.

Re-estimating phi on a rolling basis, rather than once, turns Chapter 2's core statistic into a structural-break detector: a sudden jump toward or past 1 signals the reversion process itself has changed.

Five practical warning signs, rolling phi jumps, volatility that won't revert, a sloping moving average, a specific fundamental catalyst, and a run of failed reversions, together form a usable, non-academic checklist.
A run of failed reversions on one stock is the most directly actionable signal, since it requires no forecasting or outside research, only honest attention to a strategy's own results.
Lesson 2 turns to a related but distinct failure mode: a market that has shifted from range-bound to genuinely trending, even without a single identifiable structural break event.
